utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to continue the examination of Witness DP36?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. There's something I wish to raise. And after that, Mr. Mundis will also raise something in respect of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a matter that could be raised in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It concerns whether the accused gives evidence. Yesterday a meeting took place between Defence and Prosecution counsel where the Prosecution was informed by the Defence that the accused would not make his election until after the last witness in the Prosecution case was called. This morning, upon our entry into the Trial Chamber, we were handed a filing in French by the Defence on the same topic, and as best as I can discern the contents, it appears to be a confirmation of what we were told yesterday. Today is the deadline imposed by the Trial Chamber on the Defence to indicate whether the accused would be giving evidence. It's the third deadline in two weeks that has not been met, the previous deadlines being last Thursday, that deadline imposed on last Tuesday, and then Monday this week, and now today. Mr. President, I note that the filing this morning relies in part on Article 21, chapter 4 of the Statute. And having regard to that provision, it would seem that the words in particular relied upon are to the effect that the accused should be entitled to the minimum guarantee of not being compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt. So I don't know if that's of great assistance to the Defence. The Defence indicated after the direction was imposed on -- direction was given on Monday that they discerned a conflict between the two provisions of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which on the one hand allow the accused, if he so desires, to appear as a witness in his own defence. That appears at Rule 85(C). And on the other hand, Rule 65 ter, which of course requires the Defence at the outset of its case, indeed before the presentation of its case, to indicate -- to identify each of its witnesses. Mr. President, again, I wonder whether that really is of much assistance to the Defence because in my submission there is no conflict between those two provisions. In other words, of course the accused may or may not testify, but if he chooses to do so, then the Defence is obliged to indicate that before the Defence case commences. Mr. President, naturally the Prosecution continues to prepare itself for the possibility that the accused will be a witness, but what's involved here in my submission is a matter of principle. In my respectful submission, the Rules clearly require the accused to be indicated as a witness before the Defence case commences if that is his wish. And at this very late stage of the Defence case, it is unacceptable that not only the accused does not do so but the Defence ignores three set deadlines and expresses its intention at this stage to not do so until the last witness is called. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has received the submission in which the Defence asks to give a new decision, and we'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that case, might Mr. Mundis raise an issue in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday with the commencement of this witness's testimony, he was then taken to events occurring in -- or on or about the 2nd of May, 1992. The Prosecution wishes at this point to raise an objection on two grounds. First, again the Prosecution contends that this evidence, being prior to the indictment, is irrelevant, and we wish simply to reiterate for the record that the Prosecution's position that this potentially leads to a tu quoque defence, which is not permitted. And secondly, this evidence is cumulative. Let me remind the Trial Chamber, Witness Goran Vukovic, who testified without protective measures. His testimony in late October 2002, the Word transcript beginning at page 14608 and continuing for several pages thereafter. That witness testified about the precise event which this witness is currently being examined upon and which in our submission the 15 to 20 minutes that was spent on that yesterday, in light of the fact that it's both cumulative and irrelevant, the Prosecution view is that this -- that the Defence at the least should indicate the relevance of this cumulative evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you another question: Is the event as such contested by the Prosecution, apart from the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President. And that, I believe, was indicated previously when the first witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, two objections and one piece of information, objections, relevance, and the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence deems that the testimony of this witness is relevant, that is, that within the period of time that the witness is testifying about. That is, the indictment itself which says that there was a plan of the JNA to take important strategic positions in and around Sarajevo. The testimony of this witness will allow the Defence to show the Chamber that there was no such plan, and this witness will show the type and degree of pressure on the Yugoslav People's Army to withdraw from Sarajevo with all its materiel. That is the Defence's position. And for that reason, the Defence is examining the witness about these facts. And besides, the witness has spent a certain period of time, which is relevant, in view of the negotiations and meetings that the witness attended at that time which preceded the arrival of General Galic and after that the witness returned to that area. So for the sake of continuity and reliability of the witness, the Defence is examining this witness about these facts. And as for the objection regarding cumulative evidence about these facts, the Defence deems that this testimony is not cumulative, since -- I accept in one, and second and the third, but Witness Goran Vukovic did not testify about certain events which happened on the 1st and the 2nd and the 3rd, and we deem that the Prosecutions objection that it is cumulative is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, two objections and one information. The information was that the event was not contested as such. So what's the need to go through events in detail? Perhaps you can refer to that briefly. But what's the use of going into detail into events that are, as such, not contested, that they happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I understand that the Prosecutor does not contest the event. But for the Defence, it is very important to show through these events that the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Sarajevo and that it pulled out both its troops and materiel, and these witnesses can also tell us that a certain number -- that a certain part of the materiel, that is, the armament, stayed in the hands of the members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's another issue. I would say that perhaps as a guidance -- yesterday we spent quite some time on, let's say, the event of taking -- taking the personal liberty of persons, which is not contested. So the Defence could simply refer to that and ask for confirmation of the witness whether he's aware of that, and then of course the consequences and the meaning of that, putting pressure upon whoever and what the consequences were is the next subject the Defence, of course, could touch upon. Would you please keep this in mind, that if it's not contested and that whatever new elements are in the evidence, of course the Defence is entirely free to ask for it but to establish facts that were already established through other witnesses and that are not contested by the Prosecution is not of great assistance to the Chamber. Could then perhaps the -- would you please keep this in mind when you continue to cross-examine the witness. The curtains should be pulled down first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning -- or should I say dobar dan, Mr. DP36. You still can hear me in a language you understand, I take it from your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. DP36, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my last question was: After you arrived in the Sarajevo territory - and you told us that it was between the 22nd April and the 22nd of June, 1992 - at that time were you aware that the JNA had left - when I say "had left," I mean both the troops and materiel - that it had taken out its troops and materiel from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an eyewitness to this decision. When I was released from captivity, I eye-witnessed the decision that the JNA was to pull out from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I saw numerous officers from Serbia who were leaving the territory in a rush. But I must say that in April, when I arrived there, I could already see that large parts of the materiel were being pulled out even before the decision was taken that the JNA should leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. To my mind, the decision to leave such a critical territory was disastrous. And since at that time the JNA had already been condemned as an aggressor army, it was trying to avoid being qualified as such in Bosnia-Herzegovina and decided to withdraw with its troops and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP36, when you tell us this, are you aware if part of the materiel - and when I say "materiel," I mean the weaponry - has it all been pulled out from the area of Sarajevo, or do you have any knowledge if certain depots of the Yugoslav People's Army were taken? That is, did the JNA pull out all its weaponry from that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have such information. The information that I have is that during the pullout, some of this materiel was snatched from them. Why? Because people were in serious danger and they were left without any military experts who had pulled out from Sarajevo Rajlovac, so that a column that was pulling out through Visoko via Zenica, people snatched away from them such guns and in Sokolac some materiel was also taken. But this was snatching the weaponry away from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, yesterday you told us that you were with a column when the Yugoslav People's Army left its commands, and you said that UNPROFOR was also at the head of that column. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether UNPROFOR carried out its task as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was well conceived, and MacKenzie's word was trusted. However, the Muslim side brutally violated it and even the general was aghast at such an ungentlemanly and brutal gesture. I think that UNPROFOR did its utmost to pull us out safely, but unfortunately they were powerless because we were surrounded from all the surrounding buildings and trees and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence would like to show the videotape number 12, that is, the event that the Witness DP36 is telling us about. And when we see this tape -- and the Defence deems that it is relevant, although I see my learned friend on his legs. I expect an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed that the booth gave the tape back to Mr. Piletta-Zanin yesterday so that they have no tape. But apart from that -- you have got it. Yes. It would certainly have been far more efficient if you had given it this morning to the booth. Mr. Mundis, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A slight misunderstanding. Thank you, Your Honour. A slight misunderstanding between me and my co-counsel. I didn't realise that he had taken it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, worse things can happen. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution renews its objection on grounds of cumulative nature of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have we seen this part of this tape before, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's not cumulative, and you're allowed to play it. But please keep in mind my earlier words about cumulative evidence about events non-contested. I don't know what I'll see on the -- on the tape, and the Chamber would like to see it first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the videotape is 348/12, and the transcript, 348/12.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The tape may be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] They're aiming at us from all sides. The train can't pass through. The column made only 900 metres before being stopped in Dobrovoljacka Street by the Zelene Beretke (Green Berets), the Ministry of Interior Special assignment forces, Patriotic League, and members of other Muslim paramilitary formations. At the back of the column the plunder of equipment has started, officers and soldiers are already being arrested, wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I was provided -- the Chamber was provided with a transcript. I do, however, have some difficulties in identifying what part of the transcript relates to the clip just shown. The last page. As usual, I started on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is because the Defence wanted to present a lot of material. We identified this segment. But perhaps I failed to mark that it was to start on the third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I was very much concentrating on finding the source, could the tape be replayed. It's only a short -- where exactly does it start? "Voice on the radio," or -- page 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's how it was presented, just for that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It could be replayed, because I couldn't concentrate on it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From the Territorial Defence Hall a chosen mass of people accompanying the vehicle's column. Listen to the radio messages... The crowd should only sit down and stop them from passing through. Nothing else! They can't go by us! What was that? They can't pass by us. We have them in our sight from all sides. Unless you pull back the soldiers, we'll kill you off like rabbits. The people should block the army so they can't get through. The column made only 900 metres before being stopped in Dobrovoljacka Street by the Green Berets, Ministry of Interior Special assignment forces, Patriotic League, and members of other Muslim paramilitary formations. At the back of the column, the plunder of equipment has started, officers and soldiers are already being arrested, wounded, or killed. Pay attention to these conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you recognise -- could you identify the event on this video and was that the column that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It shows the narrowest part of the street here, at the head of the column, with General MacKenzie and General Kukanjac and Alija Izetbegovic were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you said you were in that column. And on the basis of your experience in Sarajevo, can you tell us which forces are concerned and how they were organised. And I'm referring to the forces that perpetrated this massacre and stopped the column, in your personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the video shows those forces, the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and the MUP. It was an MUP that consisted mostly of Muslims. And there were also criminal groups. And I know this because I was the hostage of one criminal group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And one other question about this incident: In your opinion, this attack on the column, was it a planned attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had been planned because there was a high-ranking officer of the former JNA with a megaphone. He had also been convicted as a criminal. And this act of theirs, what they did to the column, had catastrophic consequences for the way events developed in Sarajevo. And similarly, a group of soldiers were killed in Tuzla on the 16th of May, 1992, in Brdjanska Malta [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, bearing in mind the video we have seen and your answers, if I tell you that there is a position according to which the JNA planned to take over important strategic positions in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo and that it was already holding those positions at that time, what would your response be? Could you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the war, I spoke to General Kukanjac at length, and he claimed that the decision for the army to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina was a catastrophic decision and it had terrible consequences. It had been taken rapidly. It wasn't possible for him to consolidate any positions, and it didn't have this in plan. It wanted to be an army that would strive to solve the issue in a peaceful manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, could you please just answer my question. Do you know whether the JNA planned to take over important strategic positions in and around Sarajevo, and did it do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't take such positions over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you told us that on the 1st of April, 1993 you returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After leaving on the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you returned to and did you engage in the military when you returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was forced to leave on the 22nd of June, 1992. I was forced to leave the territory because I had to report to my assignment and I had to solve my family situation. I was then asked to return to my place of birth, which I did on the 1st of April, 1993. I returned to my place of birth in order to be with my friends and brothers and relatives and to share their fate. They would have despised me in my neighbourhood if I hadn't returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, the question was where you returned and whether you engaged in any military activities. Your answer was about the reasons why you left and what you did after you left. If the Defence would be interested to know, they will certainly ask you. Could you please listen carefully to the questions and answer to those questions. I'm telling you this because the Defence is under some time restraint as well, so they'd like to elicit from you the information they think is of importance for the Defence of General Galic. And if you spend time on issues they consider of less importance, then valuable time might be lost for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, since time is restricted, could you respond as briefly as possible in order to present the greatest possible number of facts, if we're talking about your stay in that territory. Were you assigned some military position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the corps command on the 1st of April, 1993, and I was assigned to the organ for morale and information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, when you received this assignment, when you were assigned to the organ for morale and information, can you tell us whom you reported to in the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it just so happened that my first meeting in Pale, as I was passing through, was with General Galic. We just greeted each other, and I had to continue to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an assistant, you said you were assigned to the organ for morale and information. Can you tell us what position you were assigned to and what were your duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the assistant to the colonel for morale. I was a chief in his department. He had already been assigned that position. But my -- the general wasn't my immediate superior. I performed duties from that field and in the department that I had been assigned to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, when you say that you performed duties at the position that you had assumed, can you tell us what sort of duties you performed as part of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the duties I performed had to do with reporting on the situation in the field. I would send these reports to the organ for morale, and then monthly reports and quarterly analysis of the situation as far as morale was concerned would be sent to the corps command. So I went into the field to see what the situation was with the soldiers, and the general supported this method, the method of going into the field and spending time with the men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you said you went into the field and that you spoke to the troops. Are you telling us that you visited the lines, the front lines of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to do. I wanted to become familiar with the terrors of war and all its aspects, and the general agreed to this desire of mine. Whenever I requested to go into the field, I did so. And this is something I did in addition to the other duties that I had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have now told us what your duties were when you went into the field, but you also said "in addition to other duties." What were the other duties that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they more or less had to do with the duties that I had to perform. But the general asked me to go and control how the peace -- how the truce was being respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to stop there for a minute and concentrate on one of your tasks. When you said that you were sent to monitor how the truce was being respected or whether it was being respected, can you tell us anything else about that? Can you tell us when you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the first week of May. The general assigned me a particular task after seeing him in the morning. He assigned this task to me and some of us from the corps. I was to go to the 1st Romanija Corps to control the cease-fire in the zone of responsibility of that brigade. I went at about 10.00. I arrived there at about 11.00 at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, before you answer my question as to how much time you spent there, can you tell us whether you know who signed the agreement on respecting the truce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My principle was to do what the superior ordered me to do, but it must have been signed by someone at a high level. But we had to respect it, and the general sent me to control this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that one of your first tasks was to go to the territory of the 1st Romanija Brigade, can you tell us where you went in particular when you went to control how the truce was being respected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the command of the 1st Romanija Brigade, and I reported to the commander. I spoke to him briefly. That was the first time I met him. I told him what my task was and pointed out that the general said that the truce had to be respected and that the army had to maintain its image.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, how much time did you spend there, and can you tell us while you were there, did you notice -- did you observe that the truce had been violated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 14.00 hours on that day, that's -- I was there until that time. I was in the operative centre with the duty officer and I listened to reports from the commanders of battalion in the field. The terrain was very difficult. It was difficult to pass through. And I listened to those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of reports you could accept and what sort of reports did you take away with you when you returned to the corps command? Was the truce violated? And if so, who violated it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was informed that the Muslim side was taking action in Berija, Brijesce, Faletici, and they were constantly taking action. And at about 1600 hours, it was reported that a soldier had been seriously wounded. His surname was Jokic. I remember this. He had been wounded in the job. I made a report when I returned to the command and then I forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you've mentioned the violation of the truce. While you were in the territory of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, can you tell us according to the personal knowledge that you have of this how often these truces were signed and to what extent were they respected during the period that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truces were signed -- well, I don't know how many were signed exactly and I don't know who signed them. I know that whenever they were signed, we were informed about this and it was forwarded to all the brigades. All the brigades were informed that they had to respect the truce. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether and how often this truce was violated? Was it in force? If you were told that it had been signed and that it should be respected, for how long was it in force? Was it at all respected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was on duty in the corps command, the reports from all the brigades which we received mentioned the fact that the truce had been violated -- the cease-fire had been violated by the enemy side. And in the corps command, not a single night passed without us hearing infantry fire in the Dobrinja area, which was constantly being attacked by the enemy. So the reports from all the brigades stated that not a single morning passed without a report arriving in a brigade according to which the cease-fire had been violated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, are you telling us that in that area there was firing on a daily basis, so to speak, or fighting on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, this testimony sounds very familiar to me. Did we hear already from many, many witnesses -- and it's my recollection that the truces were -- the cease-fires were always violated by the -- by the opposing party. I think I should check it, whether I heard it from three, five, seven, or ten witnesses. Cumulative evidence is not needed. I don't know whether the violations of the truces is contested as such, that such violations took place. I'm not saying as to whether the Prosecution agrees to whether it was only violated by one party but that violations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No. Certainly -- certainly violations took place, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that would go to the issue as to why there were to many of them negotiated and put into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean if they were all kept, then it was not necessary to conclude new. So I gave you some guidance, Ms. Pilipovic, as to cumulative evidence and repetitive evidence and issues not being contested. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you said that you were on duty in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often you were on duty in the corps command and what sort of duties did this involve when one was on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the duty officer in the corps on the basis of the list, and the duties of the duty officer included gathering intelligence reports, monitoring the situation, and controlling whether orders had been respected, the orders that were issued that morning and which were regulated even before and which have to be respected for a longer period of time. So this was one of the duties, not to mention others.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, while you were at your post as duty officer in the corps command, did you at any time receive written protests from UNPROFOR? First of all, I should ask you whether you at any time had contact with UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any personal contact with them, but I received the task from the general to lead a column of UNPROFOR vehicles through our territory via Butmir, Ilidza, Osijek, up to Vogosca, and on that trip the driver and officer who was with me was a witness when a mortar shell hit us. It came from the direction of Butmir. This was in Ilidza. This was the personal contact I had. But later on I had more contact with UNPROFOR representatives when I was in the north-western part and I had to implement certain orders with them, orders which I received from the corps, and I also had to perform certain other actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, we shall return to the issue of your cooperation with UNPROFOR when you were in the north-western part of the battlefield. But when you were the duty officer in the corps command, did you at any time receive a protest from UNPROFOR according to which an incident had happened in a certain part of the town and in which civilians had died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received such information, nor was this the practice. There was a liaison officer who received such information and then forwarded it to higher organs, and we would then receive information from the commander and his chief, but I didn't receive any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And did you at any time receive a protest from UNPROFOR while you were the duty officer? And if you did, what were the contents of those protests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was common practice, but I didn't receive any kind of protest from them. It probably wasn't up to them to inform us about that, if there was anything of that kind. But I never received such a protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you said that you spent a certain period of time in the north-western part of the battlefield. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year that covered, which brigades or units were deployed in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know which units were deployed there. That was the most critical zone in the corps because it was in certain operative surroundings. The Igman and Ilidza Brigade were there. The Rajlovac Brigade was there - which was later transformed - The Vogosca Brigade and the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you said that this area was in the operative -- in an operative circle. Can you tell us what this means, "an operative circle," "operative surroundings," with regard to the units that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. It was in an operative encirclement surroundings because the forces that were there had operational significance. But the depth surrounding it wasn't very great. It had -- it almost had two fronts. It had one front which went from Herzegovina towards Pazarici and had a front over Kiseljak, had a front towards Kiseljak, and had a front at Igman. That was from one side. And on the other side there was a front towards the part of Sarajevo that was in Muslim hands. So it was a very difficult, and there was a lot of psychological pressure for both the civilians and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you have now described that part of the front to us, and you said that while you were in that area -- well, first of all, could you tell us how much time you spent in this area and which period did this concern, given that you said in August 1994 you left the territory of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a little less than a year there, ten and a half months, I think. I was sent there at my request. I wanted to spend time in the territory over there. And secondly, I was there because the truce had been violated again. At sometime in mid-June the line moved in favour of the Muslims. It moved for 300 metres in the Vis area, in the Mijatovic Kosa area, Zabrdje area. They moved the line about 300 metres. And when the general decided that he had to form a strong unit there that could organise a better defence of that area because it was in that area that the Muslim forces approached the forces that went through Visoko, Breza.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, I'll stop you there. How often did you visit the positions in that part of the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost daily. I used all of my available time to tour that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were able to survey and see what the weaponry of Republika Srpska army was, or rather, what was the weaponry used by the members of the 1st Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the infantry weaponry, and I omitted to tell you that in that operative encirclement what was very unfavourable was that all of our lines were inferior in comparison to the Muslim lines. The Muslim lines -- the Muslims pressured us with their positions. They mostly had mortars, light machine-guns, M-71 -- M-51. But I was mostly interested in infantry weapons and in infantry troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were interested mostly in infantry troops, in these positions were you able and did you ever see snipers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither saw them nor did I wish to see them, because to me a sniper is something terrible. I never saw a sniper either in the corps or at the lines which I toured.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you tell us, during the time that you spent in the corps, do you know whether at the level of the corps command or at some meetings there were certain agreements that were signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreements were signed. There was an agreement, and I learned of this later. I didn't see that document. I learned this through the book of Michael Rose, that there had been some anti-sniper agreement that had been signed in 1994. There were number of agreements but they were not generally signed at the level of the corps command. It was mostly signed at the strategic, political level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you toured the front lines at the north-west sector of the battlefield, you told us that you were interested only in infantry troops and in infantry weaponry. But can you tell us whether there had been any heavy weapons in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there had been heavy weapons there but at the north-western side. And it was used only exclusively for defence as infantry support. Later on at the end of February 1994, that weaponry was pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that that weaponry was pulled out in late February 1994. Can you tell us whether that weaponry was pulled out based on some decision or document. What do you know about the pullout of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the weapons that were pulled out, 12.7 and up calibre, was pulled out pursuant to the resolution of the United Nations following a massacre that remains unproven still in Markale or some place similar to that. I don't know exactly. But we had to carry out that order, and it was very difficult for us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, did you personally participate in any way in the execution of this order? And if so, when was that during the pullout of the heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in charge of the north-western area, and I was in charge of controlling the speed with which this was pulled out. We were in a difficult situation. Our people were constantly in danger because the line could have been pierced, penetrated. And we went to various depots which were some 20 kilometres away, and I had to remain in contact with UNPROFOR forces in that north-western area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, you put a question to the witness. I didn't want to interrupt you earlier, but you did put a question to the witness as to agreements signed. And it's my recollection that I heard that you asked about anti-sniping agreements, where in the transcript it appears that -- was it in general about agreements?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general about agreements. And Mr. DP36 said that he knew about the agreements and he also mentioned one of the agreements that was signed in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was aimed at the agreement on withdrawal of heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may add, I simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... It was in the answer that the anti-sniper agreement was -- I -- I have to apologise. It was the answer, rather than the question. So the transcript seems to be complete. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, you told us that you participated in the execution of -- in the implementation of the agreement on withdrawal of heavy weapons in the north-western area of the front. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not participate in that. I was simply in charge of implementation. I was not authorised to sign anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you told us that you were tasked with implementation, can you tell us who assigned this task to you and was this agreement implemented, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ask both of you to slow down, because if we want to hear whatever you say, Mr. DP36, then the interpreters should have an opportunity to -- a possibility to translate your words. Yes. I can imagine that it's quite understandable that this happens. Ms. Pilipovic, would you please keep this in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. DP36, can you please answer the question. Who issued that order or task to you, and can you tell us whether that agreement was implemented successfully. Did you carry out your assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assignments or tasks are usually issued by the corps commander to the people in brigades, and then we would in turn receive it from the brigade commander or the tactical group that existed and we simply had to implement it. There was no other alternative. The agreement was implemented with difficulty, but the commander of UNPROFOR forces at the time, General Michael Rose, agreed with this observation. So we carried out that with difficulty, but we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you told us that you spent some time in the corps command, which is located in Lukavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, according to you, General Galic had a good view of the city of Sarajevo from his command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no way he could have had a good view of the city of Sarajevo. One could have such a view but not from General Galic's premises. Only when one would go out, one would be able to see the Dobrinja area, and only in winter or fall when there were no leaves on the trees, and also a part of Hrasnica, because we had Mojmilo in between.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, while you spent time in the corps command as a duty officer, you told us that you received reports. As a duty officer, did you also receive certain orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were there to do our job and to be informed about the entire situation, and we would normally receive orders from the corps commander, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were given orders, can you tell us whether at any time you received or heard that General Galic, if it was him who personally issued an order -- of an order -- so did you ever hear or did you ever receive an order that a fire be opened against civilians who lived in the area under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is out of the question. General Galic or any other officer could not have issued such an order. I never received such an order from General Galic myself nor did he ever think of ordering anything of that nature, nor did I hear ever during our briefing that there was an intention of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You just told us that you never heard something of that nature during your briefings. Can you tell us whether you were present, and if so, how often, at the meetings where General Galic attended as well, and what kind of briefings did you receive there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was at the corps command, I was invited to the briefings, although technically there was no obligation to invite me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether General Galic respected or observed the views presented by his men at the briefings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his methodology was to listen to his subordinates, and that was the mechanism of his decision-making. While listening to his subordinate, operatives, assistants and so on, he would create a decision in his head and his word would be final. And I believe that this is a proper way to make decisions. We generally did not have any objections after the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, in view of the time that you spent in the corps and in view of the fact that you attended morning meetings and so on, can you tell us what was the position, what was the attitude of General Galic with respect to the cease-fire agreements, truce agreements, and so on, the agreements on humanitarian aid, on the passage of humanitarian aid convoys? What was the attitude of General Galic with respect to these agreements that had been signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the general had to carry out the orders received from the general staff, from his superiors. General Galic had quite a number of problems because humanitarian aid arrived in his territory in the part of Sarajevo held by Muslims, and these problems were not the problems created by the army. These problems were the problems relating to the population, because through this humanitarian aid military equipment arrived as well. And Your Honour, if you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, we will get to that issue about your personal knowledge regarding the transport of humanitarian aid into the part of town controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Tell us, please: Do you personally know of any abuses of humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to tell you that, that there were several instances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Cumulative. We've heard a wealth of evidence relating to what the Defence characterises as abuse of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, if we first will try to find out whether that evidence is corroborated or not by this witness and if there's any detail that was not yet in evidence, please ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. At any rate, Mr. DP36 corroborates the testimony of the protected witness. I can't tell you the pseudonym -- the initials of that witness because I do not recall them right now. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Mundis, would there be any objection against leading if it relates to earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you can lead the witness through the main elements of the testimony -- the evidence that has been presented before. And if there is anything additional that's not yet presented to the Chamber, please feel free to ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, were you present at a certain place -- and I am specifically interested in Kasindolska Street when the humanitarian convoy was halted and when the equipment was found in the convoy that was supposed to be taken in the part of territory controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I hope you will allow me to state the following: I was never personally present at the site where this happened. However, after I read the book called "The clever strategy," written by the commander of the TO army, Sefer Halilovic. At page 94 he boasts and says that they tricked us and managed to use the humanitarian aid to supply weapons and ammunition to Sarajevo. This is on page 94. The book is called "The clever strategy," by Sefer Halilovic. I just wanted to state that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP36. Can you tell us, in view of the fact that you toured the front lines, according to you what was the operative position of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that was the most difficult position of any unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. I can give you details if the Presiding Judge will allow me. First of all, they were inferior in terms of their numbers and in view of the unit surrounding them. They had to carry out very difficult defence operations so that the Muslims would not take up the plant in Hadzici that they could have used in order to carry out a very brutal revenge operation. So the corps did their best in order to prevent that. I had an opportunity to speak to the general, and I heard that the corps had absolutely no ability to carry out aggression. It was only involved in defence because of its position, of its equipment, and of its forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, you told us that in addition to the tasks you had in the field, with respect to the observation of cease-fire agreements, and in addition to your contacts with UNPROFOR and your duties as duty officer, you were also assistant to the commander for morale and information. Did you have any other tasks during the time you spent in that area, and what were those tasks, the area held by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those tasks mostly pertained to keeping the morale of the forces at a satisfactory level and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, I will stop you there. Did you personally have any information concerning what facilities were used to house the members of the BH army in the part of town controlled by their forces? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information. I did not receive it. However, I heard that they mostly used inhumane firing positions, or rather, that they placed their positions in the vicinity of humanitarian buildings and structures. We heard a lot about that, and this is also confirmed by General Michael Rose. He said that he found a lot of Muslim firing positions in inappropriate places in the vicinity of kindergartens, schools, hospitals, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. DP36, do you personally know whether at the corps level there had been meetings of, so to say, certain commissions? That is to say, do you know whether there had been any mixed commissions set up by warring sides, and were you ever present at the meetings of such commissions, and what took place there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that at the strategic level, there were commissions and at the operative tactical level the corps command had its organs and their composition varied. On one occasion, I was assigned to attend negotiations at the airport. There were some difficult questions discussed there. I went with General Tolimir to attend these negotiations at the airport. And at the level of the corps command, there was a commission which I think had a variable composition. And on one occasion I was tasked with going to these negotiations at the airport with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, so you were sent to attend negotiations with General Tolimir. Was that the meeting of the commission at the level of the general staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was delegated to attend in order to learn what were the corps' tasks regarding that. The convoys of Muslims and Croats were to leave the town and cross our territory, and this is what was discussed there. General Tolimir agreed to this. However, they did not manage to reach an agreement regarding that. General Tolimir even offered buses to them. A lot of people wanted to leave Sarajevo. General Tolimir was very understanding. He offered them to use our buses and cross our territory. However, they were unable to reach an agreement. I think this was one of the last meetings chaired by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, do you know what was the position of the corps command -- what was the attitude of the corps command with respect to organising and enabling the civilian population to pass through the territory held by Sarajevo Romanija Corps? Do you personally know whether there had been such instances when the civilian population passed through that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command was not authorised to pass decisions concerning whether they would be allowed to pass through the territory. That was done at the higher level. Whereas, the corps command had to enable them unhindered passage through that area. Therefore, General Galic was not authorised to decide who was to be let through and who wasn't. He simply carried out orders issued by superior organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information as to whether there had been such passages and whether unhindered passage was enabled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking now about the time when General Michael Rose was there. There had been convoys. There had been passages, and I believe that there were no incidents, at least in the area held by the corps. Whoever wanted to leave, if a prior agreement existed, was able to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your contacts in the north-western part of battlefield, your contacts with UNPROFOR I mean, and contacts relating to the passage of humanitarian convoys, what was your attitude regarding the cooperation with UNPROFOR members, their cooperation with the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal attitude is extremely positive. I have my own personal attitude. We desired such cooperation. However, I can't tell you about the level above, although I have to quote the words of General Michael Rose once again, who said verbatim --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would like to raise an objection in the presence of -- in the absence of the witness, perhaps, given that it's close to a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could do that then now and have a break. Therefore, I'd like to ask the usher to pull down the curtains and ask the -- escort the witness out of the courtroom. Witness DP36, we'll have a break for approximately half an hour, and there's one procedural issue we'll have to discuss and we'll discuss it in your absence. So we'd like to see you back in half an hour. Is there -- Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. All I wanted to say is that this was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your last question, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be any reason, then, to hear your objection, Mr. Mundis? Is it about questions and answers already been given, or would it be for future questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It has to do with answers already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Upon your return, then, you'll be further examined by counsel for the Prosecution, and perhaps there will be questions from the Bench as well. Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be very brief, in light of both the break and the fact that Ms. Pilipovic has no further questions. But for the record, the Prosecution objects to several of the answers. And I know that's not the normal course of events. But on four occasions this witness referred to material that he's read in books, including three references to Sir Michael Rose's book, and one reference, including a page number to Sefer Halilovic's book. And the Prosecution objects to this type of evidence on the grounds that it has the effect of getting into evidence, material which may not otherwise be admissible, or evidence which the Defence could have put to Sir Michael Rose when in fact he was here testifying. So we simply raise an objection to this type of evidence. And I understand it came in response -- or it may not have necessarily come in response, but for the record we object to witnesses coming in, citing to page numbers of books as an improper means of giving evidence before the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, I do understand that the Prosecution does not blame the Defence for eliciting such information from the witness. Having heard that he worked for a long time as a military historian, it's perhaps not a major surprise that he gives answers where he uses sources which historians might easily use. Would you respond to that, and let's just limit ourselves to the objection that -- how to evaluate or how to consider this evidence when -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence deems that the testimony of this witness was a fact testimony. He testified about the events about which he knew personally, and we believe that in his testimony he wanted to corroborate what he personally knew by using the material that pertained to that period of time and by using the quotations he gave us here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, may I just ask you: Did I understand the testimony of this witness well. For example, when he referred to one of these books, that he started answering that he does not have -- he was never present but that he read in a book what someone else said about it? Your answer is that he invoked the references in the books to corroborate what he personally had observed or what his personal knowledge was. Whereas, I -- I could check it, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I remember one such answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I think where the witness said first -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I remember that answer. We spoke about abuses of humanitarian aid. And my question was whether Mr. DP36 was present at any event. I think I mentioned Kasindol instance, because we heard prior testimony regarding that. And the witness didn't say that he didn't know about that event but that he knew that there had been such instances and that this is also confirmed by the book of Mr. Halilovic, meaning the abuses. He didn't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check, then, his exact answer. Ms. Pilipovic, upon your question on the Kasindolska Street incident, the witness answered: "Mr. President, I hope you will allow me to state the following. I was never personally present at the site where this happened. However, after I read the book called "The clever strategy," written by the commander of the TO army, Sefer Halilovic at page 94 --" you could hardly say that this is corroboration of what he personally experienced, because he says he wasn't present there. He doesn't make any reference to the occurrence of -- at least in this answer. But I take it in general terms - but the Chamber will consider it - that at least where the witness refers to books that he establishes as a fact of personal knowledge that this appears in a book and the book mentioned. If we would further have to establish the truth of what is written in the books, it might not be sufficient to just ask someone what is written in a book. I think if we keep that in mind, then we'll certainly -- but of course, you could say that the mere fact that someone writes it in a book gives, at least, a beginning of evidence or some suspicion that it might be true that at least someone has thought about this as being the truth. But whether this would be the final evidence or what is written in books -- similar when I keep in mind the exchange of views of the parties and remarks of a lot of witnesses on the possibilities of distortion of the truth in reports, whether these are media reports, whether these are written books -- I think it's a fact of common knowledge that a subjective approach to facts is, at least, a possibility when you write a book, when you make a film, and I think that this is of such general knowledge that the parties would agree that that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I merely wished to mention that Witness DP36 at the relevant time of the indictment was in the area. And in view of his combat orders, we believe that he had information that such incidents did take place. And whether he was personally present, well, we heard it from him. But the Defence nevertheless believes that the witness was informed about all the incidents of that nature, such as the abuses of humanitarian aid, in view of his rank and his presence at morning briefings. In other words, I again still believe that he merely -- that when he quoted books, he merely wanted to corroborate that in his view that was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be wise that if you -- you did not always ask him about his personal knowledge. For example, on this event, on the abuse of humanitarian aid. He said, "Well, let me just say it's in the books." If you would need to elicit from him the information you are telling us now, that apart from what he testified already about on the basis of his personal knowledge that there would be other areas where he would have personal knowledge and not just knowledge taken from books. Your estimate was that you would need four hours. Of course -- the there would still be some time if you would like to elicit this information from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, well --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is an error. We have envisaged two hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even then there would be some time left in order to come to your two hours. I'm not insisting on you using the full two hours. But since there -- you take a different position from the Prosecution and that you understand the testimony to be the corroboration of personal knowledge, personal observation of events, knowledge obtained by other means than by reading books, perhaps it would be wise to have this clarified in a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I will ask him that question after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ask him then about facts. Yes? We'll adjourn until ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I was informed that you'd like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly. In relation to the issue of the accused perhaps giving evidence, a practical consequence of not knowing for the Prosecution is the difficulty it creates in planning out cross-examination of the other remaining witnesses given the tight time constraints on our cross-examination. If we did know, then we could plan our cross-examination much more efficiently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the request of the Prosecution to give a new decision on when to decide whether the accused, General Galic, would testify as a witness. The Chamber has noticed that the Defence has until now postponed its decision whether or not to call the accused as a witness. The Chamber also notes that the Defence has not provided any summary of the evidence to be given by the accused, General Galic, as a witness. The Chamber respects the difficulties the Defence has to, when reaching a decision on whether or not to call General Galic as a witness. On the other hand, the Chamber has also taken into consideration the difficulties the Prosecution Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18068 to 18075. is facing in preparing cross-examination in case General Galic would testify; and therefore, the Chamber takes the position that the Prosecution should be properly informed in order to -- that all information is provided to the Prosecution necessary in order to prepare for the cross-examination. Therefore, if the Defence wants to reserve its right to call General Galic as a witness, they should provide a detailed survey of subjects the accused would testify about to the Prosecution. That should be done as soon as possible. The Defence has several times indicated that they would come up with a decision. They now ask for more time, but it should be as soon as possible. The detailed survey of the subjects the accused will testify about should be provided to the Prosecution. The Defence should call the accused before it calls expert witnesses to testify. Even if the accused will be the last to testify of these witnesses of fact, his testimony should be available when the expert witnesses are examined. If, finally, the Defence will decide not to call General Galic, the Chamber will accept that he will not be called up till that moment. That means he will be, apart from any exceptions of non-availability of witnesses of fact or that they could not be summoned in time, but as a principle the Defence should have made up its mind before we start hearing expert witnesses. If, for whatever reason, on the basis of the testimony still to be heard after that there would be a need to re-call General Galic after the expert witnesses have been examined, the Defence may apply for a re-call. That is the ruling of the Chamber on this issue. So to say it in short, if you want to reserve the right, the Defence should enable the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination, and General Galic should be examined before the expert witnesses. The Defence is invited to inform the Chamber about the time they would need to provide the detailed survey of subjects they would like to examine General Galic as a witness about. And as I said before, it should be done as soon as possible. We'd like to know when the Defence thinks it could provide that survey. Not necessarily at this very moment, but as soon as possible. And having in mind that the Defence indicated that the last witnesses of fact might be heard on the 28th of January, and keeping in mind the time needed for cross-examination, that "as soon as possible" would mean very soon. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, given that today's date is the 22nd and, therefore, it's -- it seems that we are already approaching, if not within, the seven-days' notice that the Defence must give for the calling of witnesses who are confirmed on the witness list, it's my respectful submission that not only the 65 ter summary of evidence to be heard but also the time estimate should be given to the Prosecution very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When I said "as soon as possible and that would be very soon," you will understand that if the Prosecution would need more time, we'll consider that. But as a starting point, the testimony should be heard before we start with the expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respectfully propose that there be a particular date by which that information is to be conveyed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I first would like to hear when the Defence thinks it could do so. Today is Wednesday. Let's -- let's hear this -- if you want to consult, Ms. Pilipovic, with General Galic and perhaps with co-counsel, I think it would be a good idea to hear from you at the start of the hearing tomorrow morning, not later than that. And please keep in mind when I say "soon," I am talking about seven days usually as the time limit for indicating calling order and exhibits, not about summaries that are provided for other witnesses already at a previous stage. And keeping the mind the time schedule, that it's really to be done very quickly. Yes? Then if there are no further questions on this issue, could we please have the witness into the courtroom again, Madam Usher. I hope that there's no misunderstanding. Just one of my -- my fellow Judges asked me. There is up till the last moment an opportunity to say "We will not call General Galic." But all preparations, if you want to reserve the right to call him -- all preparations should be -- should continue such that the Prosecution would be fully prepared to cross-examine General Galic, if he will be called. So it's a matter of reserving the right. That's what you asked for. And the Chamber has decided that you're allowed to do so if full opportunity will be given to prepare for testimony. And you know the date, before the expert witnesses, which is rather soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, by way of clarification, I assume that that means that in the case of the accused, the seven-day notice doesn't apply. If the Defence is to have its options open up until the last moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They should enable the Prosecution to prepare -- well, I mean, finally if -- even when the last witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. -- Will have testified. And at that moment the Defence will decide that it's refraining from calling General Galic, they could do that up till that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please -- Ms. Pilipovic, would you have further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not surprised by it. There might be some more questions before you will be

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, before the break we were talking about the abuse of the humanitarian aid convoys. And I asked you -- I asked you about one specific incident. So my question to you now is: During your tour of duty as assistant chief for morale, did you ever receive information that a humanitarian aid convoy had been abused in an area where its unfettered passage to the city of Sarajevo had been authorised? So did you personally receive such information? If not, did you hear about it? And if you did hear it, then who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Leading, compound questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would not lead, please, Ms. Pilipovic, that would be far better.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll put the question to the witness. You referred to the book of Sefer Halilovic in respect of the abuse of humanitarian aid convoys. What would you know about it, apart from these books? What information did you get while performing your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I did not receive this information. But this information arrived at the corps command from the Ilidza Brigade, and that is how I was -- how I knew about this information, and it was also shown on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say you didn't receive the information but it arrived at the corps command and that's how you knew about it, how did the information come from the corps command to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you learned that at the morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the meetings, you were orally informed about these events; is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly was told to you about the incident you heard about? How many were there? -- Perhaps as a first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not always learn of these incidents. I learnt about that incident which happened at Ilidza. But there were a number of such incidents. But I was no longer interested in it, but there were abuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This incident in Ilidza, what did you learn about that during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no details presented at the briefings. Only the report said that with the humanitarian food delivery, ammunition was found there, and it was shown on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You watched that television clip, or were you told that it was on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I saw it on the evening news. It had nothing to do with interest or whatever. One could see it in the evening, on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were no further details provided during the briefing or during the meeting you attended, apart from what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was when this particular case was concerned. Other cases I wasn't present, so I cannot speak about them. But be that as it may, information about the violation and abuse of humanitarian aid kept coming, and I wasn't taking decisions as to what we should do about such abuses intended to reinforce the combat preparedness of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that no further details were given during this meeting on the Ilidza incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Mr. DP36, can you tell us, since you told us there were a number of such incidents, who was it that reported at the morning briefings about events about what had happened in the territory of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main report was submitted by the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Do you remember the contents of such reports that the chief of staff submitted to the commander at the morning briefings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these reports were submitted every day, and they varied from one day to the other. I cannot remember the details.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the abuses of humanitarian relief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever such incidents occurred, the corps commander was informed about them.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you.
