utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps operational staff, can you tell us from the position that you held, your chain of command upwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Upward?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To whom did you report, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accounted to assistant commander for morale. But since as of July, I was in the north-western part of the front, I was subordinated to the tactical group commander, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "the assistant commander for morale," was that person Captain Radomir Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the name of the person on the operational staff that you reported to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know why the Vogosca Tactical Group was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that qualification about criminal information, I'd like to support with additional facts when it comes to cumulative information. So cumulative information was about the violations and non-compliance with cease-fire agreements. In Vogosca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether evidence is cumulative or not is for the Chamber to decide, because we know what evidence we heard and you might not be aware of all the evidence this Chamber heard. So would you please answer the question whether you know why the Vogosca Tactical Group was established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, I assure you. But I wanted to provide you with specific information which you probably did not get from other witnesses, Mr. President. But now I will answer the question of the Prosecutor. That group was formed, and it was of a temporary, provisional group, an ad hoc group, and it was formed in order to strengthen the defence of that particular axis, of that direction, to make the deployment of forces more forceful and more rational, because they were few in strength and they were both physically and mentally exhausted and it had no other purpose. So it was ad hoc in nature, and its commander was made of and strengthened with the staff from the corps, with personnel from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know when the Vogosca Tactical Group was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ordered to report there on the 11th of July, and the decision to form it was taken one or two days before that. I wouldn't know the exact date, but I suppose it was sometime in the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that was 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time when the Vogosca Tactical Group was formed, what was the name and rank of the commanding officer of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Lieutenant Colonel Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which units were subordinated to the Vogosca Tactical Group when it was established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made of Vogosca Brigade, Ilijas Brigade, and brigades on their flanks which were not brigades in terms of formations but they were called "brigades." They were more like battalions, and they were Rajlovac and Kosevo Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us earlier this morning that these units were in the most critical zone of the corps. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown the map which has been marked P3644.DP36. And I would ask that that be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate what part. It's a rather large map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like the witness -- perhaps he can assist the usher in showing the part of the map where the Vogosca Tactical Group was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, on the map that you have before you, do you see the areas where the Vogosca Tactical Group was operating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly the positions and front lines, but this map -- I'm slightly short-sighted. I can't see it quite clearly, but I can answer those questions orally, without the map, since I know all the boundaries, areas of responsibility and all that. It was from Pilicara, Brijesce to Grdonj feature in this part here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Towards Sarajevo, which belongs to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps turn to the microphone. And perhaps the usher could assist, because you are bending over to the -- yes. And could you please slow down so that every word will be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry that I cannot point at it on the map, because the map is not sufficiently clear. But I can tell you orally. So in the west, the last point was Pilicara, the so-called Pilicara railway depot. And that was its right-hand line. And the last left-hand side was at the Grdonj feature that was next to Mrkovic. And then on towards Visoko, its responsibility extended from so-called Stijena, which is below Ostrik feature and Crkvica, northward to north, north-west. Then following the Bosna River and then across Cemerska Mount almost to Zvijesda Mount. That was the area of responsibility of that tactical group and it was quite long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long was the front line that this tactical group had responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the part of the city which belonged to Sarajevo. I believe that this front line was about 18 kilometres. And the one towards north, north-west, it was much longer and it was close to 80 kilometres. I cannot be quite exact because the lines were -- zigzagged. They went up dales and down vales, but they were close to 70 kilometres on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm still not clear, witness. Was it as you have described effectively two fronts or was it the most critical zone in the corps for some other reason or reasons, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, the Muslim lines were the closest to each other. That is, above the road from Semizovac to Nisici plateau on Greda, which is feature Lipa and then along the mountain saddle, Mosevacko Hill, that was held by Muslim forces which were threatening and targeting the road which led to Nisici plateau. From that frontline, that is above the Semizovac-Nisici plateau road to the front line Hotonj to Mrkovici as the crow flies is less than 4 kilometres, so that is the line of their approach was almost 80 kilometres. And the Muslim forces could threaten us there and cut it off very easily, and then this whole western part of the area with almost 100.000 people could have been easily cut off and completely isolated from the Romanija plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that among your responsibilities were standing duty in the corps command. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Within the corps, what were the qualifications to stand duty as the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For somebody to stand duty as a duty officer, he naturally had to have graduated from the military academy, and it was also highly desirable to have come out from the higher military academy, and those with higher military knowledge, they were chief duty officers. But there were also cases that we had as duty officer people who were lieutenant colonels. Yet they were up to that kind of duty, because they had sufficient -- they had had sufficient training and education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your recollection, how many officers in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the operational staff met those qualifications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are different values. Some were more capable; some were less capable. But more or less we were all capable of serving as duty officers and monitoring the situation on the ground because we had to know the situation in the field in order to be able to propose operative solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please provide for the Trial Chamber the names and ranks of any other officers within the operational staff of the corps who also stood that duty, to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am a protected witness after all, and I cannot answer these questions. I have -- I am up to a number of problems in my life, and I have very many difficulties to grapple with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session, that the answer becomes known to the Prosecution but not to the outside world. Is that what you would prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's confirmed on my screen. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us this morning that you attended morning briefings at the corps. Do you recall approximately how many such briefings you may have attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said at the beginning. It was possible for me not to go to those meetings, but the general always asked me to come. He thought that I was an educated man. An educated man should attend those meetings. And he asked me to attend the meetings, which I accepted. It was some sort of recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you: The question was how many you would attend. You've explained why you attended but have given no answer to the question. May I again ask you to carefully listen to the question and answer the question. If there's any additional information you certainly asked about or if it's really of vital importance, tell us. But first of all concentrate on what you were specifically asked for. The question was: How many, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take the number of 100, then I was at 80 per cent of those briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, Witness, you estimate that you attended 80 such morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 80 per cent of such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you also told us that there were approximately 100 meetings. And 80 per cent of 100 is 80, to my knowledge. But if you would disagree, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count the number of briefings. They took place every day when the general was in the corps command. And out of all those meetings, I went to 80 per cent of them. I didn't say there were 100 such meetings. The morning meetings were obligatory. These briefings were given by the general every day when he was in the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again, your first answer was, "If we take the number of 100, then I was at 80 per cent of those briefings." A percentage is irrespective of the original number, as you might know, so how many -- the simple question is: Approximately how many of those briefings you attended? Would it be 20, 40, 60, 150? Just give us an approximate number of how many of these meetings you attended. That's what you were asked for. Ms. Pilipovic -- or is there a translation problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to avoid any confusion, with your permission, perhaps we should just mention the time that Mr. DP36 spent in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was just asked how many of these meetings he attended. I take it that it was when he was at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear to me. The question is clear to me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like just to have an answer to the questions put to you. So how many of these, approximately, of these meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was in the corps for three months, whenever I was there -- but often I was in the field. It could have been 30 or 40, but perhaps even 60 times during that three-month period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were all of the meetings that you attended at the corps held at the Lukavica barracks, in the headquarters of the corps, in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only place where morning briefings were held in the corps command. That's as far as the corps is concerned. But when I was in Vogosca, the general came on several occasions to Vogosca to our meetings with the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions do you recall the general coming to the briefings at the Vogosca Tactical Group? Can you be more specific than several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than ten times, two or three times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were with the Vogosca Tactical Group and General Galic came, do you recall on each of these occasions approximately how long he stayed in the area of responsibility of the Vogosca Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to the north-western part. And since that was the only route, the command of the tactical group would be the first place. He would stay there as long as he thought it was fit. Then he'd go to Ilidza, Hadzici, Rakovica. He would meet the commander. They would speak to each other. They would meet alone as commanders. He wanted to be familiar with the entire situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So that we're clear on this, Witness, when General Galic would come and meet with the commanders, you're telling us that he would meet alone with the commanders, one on one, during these visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. When he came, he would speak to the commander. But later he would call everyone and then there would be a briefing, a reporting. They would inform on the situation. But naturally before the meeting, he would speak to the commander. Not everyone had to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'll read back what the transcript said. It said -- this is line 21, page 58. "He would meet the commander. They would speak to each other. They would meet alone as commanders." Did General Galic meet one on one, alone with the brigade commanders of these brigades that you've mentioned, in these locations you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he ever met them alone in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let's return now to the meetings that occurred -- the corps briefings that occurred at Lukavica barracks. During the meetings that you were present at at which General Galic presided, do you ever recall the topic of protests concerning unlawful shelling being discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember how the general reacted towards the end of the month of May. I think it was Saturday or Sunday. I don't know for certain. I know how he reacted when his command was subjected to mortar shelling from Kovaci, and Butmir he asked for General Indjic to be found urgently and to contact UNPROFOR, to caution UNPROFOR, to have UNPROFOR caution the Muslim side that they had started shelling us for no reason while we were in the command. Mr. President, if I may go into additional details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just ask you a couple of questions about this so that I understand. General Galic was in his command headquarters which then received incoming fire? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were exposed to mortar shelling, that there was an attack. I was there. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And General Galic's response was to contact UNPROFOR to relay this information to the opposing side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And that's why Major Indjic had to react very rapidly in order to prevent the situation from escalating. But that's not how it ended. Afterwards there was an attack and the road between Lukavica and Pale was cut off by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the part near Vidikovac on Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just ask you a couple more questions about this. Was -- based on your understanding of this situation in which General Galic contacted Major Indjic -- did General Galic consider that his command headquarters was not a legitimate military target; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't think that. The corps command is a legitimate target, but not if there is a truce which is in force. That was a hidden attack -- a concealed attack in order to cut off the road from Lukavica to Pale on Trebevic and to draw attention to other things. That was done on that day and it was very difficult for us to re-establish that route in order to have a passage to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me return to the meeting --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in order to disturb the functioning of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to the meetings at Lukavica barracks. At these meetings in which both yourself and General Galic were in attendance, did you ever hear anyone at any of these of these meetings discuss protests concerning the unlawful sniping of civilians on the other side of the confrontation line; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at any time, at any location, did you ever hear General Galic complain about protests that he received from any source concerning unlawful shelling; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did that through the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm talking now about General Galic complaining about protests he received concerning shelling by forces under General Galic's control into the territory held by the opposing side. Did you hear him complain about protests that he received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything about such protests being discussed. I don't know what you mean. That his forces were fighting in the town? Is that what you mean? Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me try to rephrase the question. Did General Galic ever complain to you or in your presence about protests that he received from the United Nations about unlawful shelling of Bosnian Muslim civilians? And when I say "complain about these protests," for example, he may have said something along the lines of "this is unfair. We're being subjected to these protests without a basis," et cetera. Did he ever vocalise a complaint about protests that he received concerning shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I wasn't present in such situations, but I do know that he didn't receive -- so I don't know how to answer that question. It wasn't for me to discuss this matter. All I know is that the general never mentioned that the urban part of the town should be shelled. He never even thought about this. And I can confirm this because on one occasion we spoke at length, and I saw that there was no animosity on the part of the general, neither on an ethnic basis or a religious basis towards the enemy side. It would have not been logical for him to order someone to be shelled. So I never heard anything about this from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be clear. There seems to be some misunderstanding. Let me put the question to you in a different way. Did you ever hear that General Galic, for example, said, "They're blaming us for shelling civilians without any good basis for that"? So was there ever any complaint by General Galic on either UNPROFOR blaming your forces for illegal violence against civilians? I'm not talking about whether these would be complaints that were justified or not but whether there was ever any mentioning made of "they're blaming us for..." Not whether General Galic ordered such attacks, not whether they were true or not, but whether he ever expressed that he was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that. That can only be the field of the liaison officers who have to deal with UNPROFOR. They could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just quite -- be quite clear to you. The question was not whether ever such complaints have been lodged, but the question was whether you ever heard General Galic expressing whatever on such complaints. That is not a question that could only be answered by liaison officers. That is a question about whether you ever heard General Galic expressing himself on such complaints in whatever way, either by complaining about that these complaints were lodged or discussing the -- whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anything about those protests, and I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago it appears from the transcript that you started a sentence and then didn't finish it. You said, "I do know that he didn't receive." Do you recall what you were referring to when you said "I do know that he didn't receive"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At morning briefings we never heard anything about any protests which had been forwarded to our side by UNPROFOR or through other channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You're telling us, Witness, that you -- at no point in time did you ever hear a discussion about protests from the UN or UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, earlier this morning in response to a question from Ms. Pilipovic -- the question was: "Did you at any time receive a protest from UNPROFOR according to which an incident had happened in a certain part of the town in which civilians had died?" The answer was: "I never received such information, nor was this the practice. There was a liaison officer who received such information and then forwarded it to higher organs, and we would then receive information from the commander and his chief." You're telling us that that information was not discussed at the morning briefings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss it. We were simply always told that we have to observe the truce and that we should never be those who start the first, and we abided by this principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when you said this morning "There was a liaison officer who received such information and then forwarded it to higher organs," which higher organs did the liaison officer forward this information to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that with full certainty. All I can say is that I assume that it is normal for it to go upper, first to the corps command and then to upper echelons. I never went to inquire about this with the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you then said: "Then we would then receive information from the commander." When you said "the commander," you were referring to the corps command, General Galic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what is contentious about this. The general makes a decision based on the information which doesn't have to be disclosed to us, and he requires that we obey the order issued by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Is this the approximate time we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this would be a suitable moment for you for the break, then we'll adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom again. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I suggest to you that there was a plan of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to deliberately and indiscriminately target civilians on the other side of the confrontation line. Do you agree or disagree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely disagree. I do not believe that there was such a plan. Had I known about the existence of that plan, I would have never joined the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- In view of what the testimony was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Mr. DP36. You have told us this morning about an operative encirclement. What do you exactly understand by that term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war theory recognises tactics, operative and theory as a strategy. A zone held by a corps is usually a zone of operative significance. And in view of the forces that were positioned in the north-westerly area, they held an area that was of an operational significance and was resolving the strategic issue concerning Sarajevo. So that was a large area, with the fall of which many things would have been disturbed concerning the way we waged war at the time, defensive [Realtime transcript read in error "offensive"] war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us this morning about a view you would have from the Lukavica barracks. You said if you would go out, you could, depending on the time of the year, see parts of Dobrinja. And then you said that Mojmilo would take the view -- would be -- would obstruct the view. Did you then refer to the view from Lukavica to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question asked was whether from the command post of General Galic there was a view of the city of Sarajevo. I said that one couldn't see Sarajevo because above Lukavica there was Mojmilo rising in the middle, and one could only see a part of Dobrinja only when there were no leaves on the trees that could obstruct the view. Basically, only in the fall and in winter. From Lukavica, one can normally see Butmir, Hrasnica, and the area close Ilidza. Physically, it's impossible to see Sarajevo. The largest part of Sarajevo, the core of it, was held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us this morning that you had never seen any snipers within the armed forces you belonged to and you didn't wish to see them because they were terrible. May I first ask you: What do you exactly understand by "snipers"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper is not a special kind of weapon. It is any weapon with an optical view that would assist in aiming. An optical device can be placed on a calibre greater than 7.6. It can be placed on 12.7, which is a greater calibre with a greater range. And larger units have special devices. This is a matter of the weaponry that an army can have, any army in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said that snipers were terrible, that you didn't want to see them, could you please explain that. And I would like to inform you that we heard evidence on two issues: First of all, that the use of snipers and/or sniper rifles is not uncommon in military units; and the second is that there has been some evidence that units would have snipers in your armed forces. And I'd like to add that sometimes sniping is referred to as firing from a distance from a concealed position with rifles. Could you please, in view of what I just told you, comment on the absence of, I would say, whatever sniper activity as I understood your testimony to be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I firmly assert that in the corps command I never saw anybody with an aiming device on a weapon. Second, as I toured the trenches in the positions held by operative tactical group Vogosca, I also never saw weapons with optical aiming devices. I only saw modified devices such as periscope, which was used to view feature 830, 850, and that was not a combat device. It was a periscope used by submarine in order to observe the area, because there was a constant threat of an infantry attack. In addition to that, when I toured front lines, in the Vogosca area from the eastern gate -- at the eastern gate I received information from the platoon commander that during one year in the area where Sucur houses were located, some 40 civilians and soldiers were killed by small arms weapons. I was not interested in investigating the issue of snipers, because I personally believe that it is an inhuman way of waging a war, using snipers. And I repeat: I never saw them while touring the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any criticism from the outside world - and I put it to you as wide as possible - on the use of sniper activities in your armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I learned about some anti-sniper agreement from the book of Sir Michael Rose. I wish to confirm your beliefs that the campaign was a monstrous campaign that was in contradiction with the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. I did not express whatever belief. This monstrous campaign you're talking about, could you tell us - because you didn't mention that before - what was that campaign? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim this with a first-hand competency because I studied this. This campaign was led on 1993 levels: Tactical, operative, and strategic one. Strategic propaganda is waged by statesmen generally. And this campaign affected us because it claimed that we were aggressors. I said to the French officer, commander of the battalion in Rajlovac, where I went many times -- I asked him whether I was an aggressor if I remained in my home area defending the house in which I was born. So this was a strategic campaign claiming that we were aggressors. The next issue was that we were terrible bad guys going around raping and killing and that we had killed some 200.000 Muslims. And this had a very bad resonance in the world where we were proclaimed to be really bad guys. At the tactical level, this campaign was reduced to deception spread out that our lines had been broken through in order to make sure that a panic ensued in our operative area, and the situation for the residents was quite difficult. We had on many occasions to go into the field to assure -- reassure the population that the lines had not been broken and to prevent the panic from being spread out. This is what I can say about this propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that part of the propaganda was that you were the aggressors and that you discussed this with a French officer. Was that an UNPROFOR officer or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you discuss this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to him in 1994. They were stationed in Rajlovac. I think the deputy commander of the battalion was Henri. We talked in general about history. I could tell that he knew a lot about history, and then I put this question to him, and he told me that he would have done the same thing; he would have gone back to his hometown and defended. And if you wish, you can bring him here so that we can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell me the name of that French officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Henri, Henry. He had quite a neutral attitude. He listened to me, and I believe that he understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that his first name or his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, whether that was his first name or his last name. That was quite a while ago, in 1994. I didn't take any notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I correctly understand your testimony to be that you asked him this question as whether he would consider someone in your position as an aggressor because that was what the propaganda war told you you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him whether I was an aggressor, if I remained in my home area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were inspired to put that question to him because that's what the propaganda said you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell me where and when did you hear the propaganda telling you that your armed forces were the aggressors.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Propaganda was present all the time. Unfortunately, it is so today, and there is constant talk of aggressors, aggression, and so on. Today's press - and I recently read it - still depicts us as aggressors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have access to those propaganda sources at that time, and what were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Main sources of such propaganda was the highest echelon of the Muslim forces, Ganic, Silajdzic, and so on. I listened to that dozens of time. I read it in the press and I heard it on television myself. Your Honours, Mr. President, one can still find that in press nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us in what press, on what television did you see that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Official television of Sarajevo and their press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you to refer to media sources on the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this has been going on continually. There wasn't just isolated instances. This propaganda is alive today, and it still depicts us as aggressors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that limited to what I would call the BiH sources, or has it been adopted by other media as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mostly propaganda activities waged by those republics that seceded from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And outside the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the International Community doesn't use that term any more. I assume that it will give its final word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "doesn't use that term any more." Did they use it in your -- according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did use it, and one can see evidence of that in the book of General Rose. It had its certain objectives in order to win over some other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm especially interested in media sources. Were you aware of international media sources at the time of the conflict when you were performing your duties, or did you only learn about them after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I followed that during the conflict. International media were openly in favour of the Muslim side, and they glorified and presented things in a manner that was quite in contradiction with the reality on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you followed these international media at that time. What media would you follow? Television or newspapers or whatever sources do you have in mind you followed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the sources that were selected from what was available internationally by the television. I wasn't in the position to read foreign press during the war. I don't speak languages well enough in order to be able to read. However, this is a matter of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say "not -- "you could not read it in the newspapers by yourself but you observed it on -- that were selected by television. Could you tell us what kind of sources these were that were selected and broadcasted, as I understand you, by television.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leading media outlets which have monopoly on the international scene and which the propaganda in Sarajevo skillfully used by taking things out of context and so on in order to undermine the morale of the Serb people in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any names of any media that were selected and subsequently broadcasted and came to your knowledge? If you don't know the names, then of course you can't tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't wish to go into any further discussions. But this is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just asking questions, and I'm not discussing with you. You say it's a fact. Was part of that media or, as you called it, propaganda campaign also the Serbs to -- the Bosnian Serbs to be blamed for sniping civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There definitely was such a campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this propaganda with any of your colleagues or within the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss this. Most of the people concluded that this is how it was. We were simply disappointed by that campaign because it was so unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, that since everyone in your environment would know for sure that it was unrealistic that that was the reason why you didn't discuss it among yourselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are merely some reflections of the very hard situation that has existed there for thousands of years. And we were confident that had anything happened of truly disastrous proportions, it would not have been us to blame for that. Because there is a certain mindset which is deeply rooted in the tradition of the three peoples living there, and that is immense mistrust, and that was the main reason why all those things happened. Because, you see, when the propaganda conveys something that is not true, it provokes the revolt on the other side, and so on and so forth, but we simply ignored this propaganda because we knew that it did not reflect the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, the Prosecution would respectfully request to ask one or two questions arising from questions put by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As usual, you are allowed to -- but limited to those issues raised by the Bench

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, in response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you told us that you personally believe that sniping is an inhuman way of waging war. I have just one or two questions about that. Let me focus not on snipers targeting civilians but the use of snipers as legitimate means of conducting arms conflict. For example, if you were seeking to take out or to engage a sniper on the other side of the confrontation line, wouldn't using a sniper be a more humane way of attacking that opposing force than, say, mortar or artillery fire, which could kill more than the intended victim or target?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, these situations require adequate solutions. I, therefore, cannot answer this question whether I would then -- because the state of war is not an ordinary state, and I wasn't in a situation to take a decision if that happened, how to eliminate a sniper on the other side. I'm talking now from a big distance, but it is up to the commander how to neutralise such a man. But one should not use inadequate or excessive means in response, but I am not aware of the cases for something like that that was targeted with a gun or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, certainly it would seem that the use of a sniper rifle to target an enemy sniper would not be excessive, given the relatively high degree of accuracy of such a weapon in the hands of a qualified sniper. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP36 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it is a pretty hypothetical question to begin with. I was not in a situation to take such a decision. I didn't know there were any snipers who could do that. So it is a hypothetical question. It is a theoretical issue that we can discuss it. It happened in the battle -- the Stalingrad battle where the snipers competed who would destroy more people on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It's just for the sake of the transcript. When answering the first question of Judge Orie involving the operative encirclement, you said the following: "So that was a large area with the fall of which many things would have been disturbed concerning the way we waged war at the time, offensive war." My question is whether you said "offensive war" or "defensive war."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said twice that General Morillon, when I talked with him, that the general said that he was never intent on waging an offensive war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question is -- because the transcript says that you mentioned "offensive war." I would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. That is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's also my recollection that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters orally said "defensive war" and that it must be a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defensive, defensive, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness DP36, this concludes your testimony in this court. You have answered all the questions of the parties and remaining questions of the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and answering all these questions, and I wish you a safe return trip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, once the curtains have been pulled down, the witness may be escorted out of the courtroom. As far as the exhibits are concerned, I take it, Mr. Mundis, that you do not insist on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please guide us through the other documents, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1837, pseudonym sheet under seal; Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted out of the courtroom. We -- I hope you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D348/3, video; Exhibit D348/3A, English transcript of video; Exhibit D348/12, videotape -- and a correction to the previous number given. The transcript is D348/12A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since there are no objections, these videos and documents are admitted into evidence. But Madam Registrar, is there any pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the first one. Oh, yes. Yes. It's before I interrupted you. Yes. I apologise. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could. I should have risen slightly earlier. With respect to the videotape and the transcript, again we would respectfully request that it be limited to that portion of the tape and transcript which was shown in the courtroom and not the remaining parts of the transcript or videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see, Ms. Pilipovic, that you are nodding, that you would agree that the admission is partial to the sense that only those parts shown and the corresponding part of the transcript is standard and, is therefore, admitted into evidence. Then is the Prosecution -- is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see. We -- I take it that we first have to -- Ms. Pilipovic, I do understand that there are no protective measures sought for your next witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the curtains may be raised, the screen may be removed. Perhaps we could already -- if the curtains are raised, that we could perhaps already ask the witness to be brought in so that we can make a start. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as Ms. Mahindaratne will be taking this witness, may I be excused from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I'd like to hear whether the Russian interpretation is available at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We hope so, Your Honour. We hope that there is an interpreter in the Russian booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Russian channel, one, two, three. The Russian interpreter is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Is the witness on the right channel, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you. I speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You speak English. Do you prefer to testify in English or do you prefer to testify in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's better for me to speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You prefer to speak English. Whenever there is any doubt as to whether you -- your mastering of the English language, both in understanding what others say and by expressing yourself, would you please inform me immediately because there is Russian interpretation available and the Chamber would highly deplore if whatever detail of your testimony would be lost by linguistic problems. Yes? It's still your preference to testify in English, I do believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to stand up and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'd first like to ask you to introduce yourself to us. So would you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: I am Sergey Moroz. What, address? Nothing else? What should I specify, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell us what kind of education you have and where do you live. When I say "education," I mean did you ever receive any military training and education?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: I graduated from the military institute. I am professional military, retired lieutenant colonel. So now I live in Kiev. I am conflict administrator in Procter & Gamble, Ukraine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moroz, you have told us that you were a lieutenant colonel, that is, that you were a military man. So now, can you tell us if as such you were engaged militarily between September 1992 and August 1994. And if so, where was that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: Since October 1993 till October 1994, I've been in UNPROFOR forces in sector Sarajevo, engineer section, mission commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, when you told us that you were a mission commander and that you were in engaged with the engineers in the UNPROFOR headquarters, could you tell us, where were you assigned -- or rather, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: I located in PTT building in Sarajevo, headquarters of sector Sarajevo. And -- well, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you tell us that you were with the engineers section, can you tell us, who was your immediate speed your, that is, your and your service's superior?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, I've been to Sarajevo for 12 months. And my -- I had two bosses, both Frenchmen, because Frenchmen had six months' rotation period. Frankly speaking, I don't remember exactly their full names. One, as far as I remember, was Patrice, and one Pierre. But frankly speaking, for me it's difficult to remember French names. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us who was the UNPROFOR sector commander in Sarajevo during your tour of duty there.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: The greater part of my stay in Sarajevo, it was General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you told us that you were engaged with the engineers section attached to the UNPROFOR forces. Can you tell us, what were your tasks in that engineers section or in your department?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, such engineer section, it was rather specific unit within the headquarters, because the main task of it was renovation of civilian objects vitally important for both warring sides -- for civilians of both warring sides. It was renovation of electricity lines, sewage system, water supply, gas. And as I was mission commander, my task was providing missions, projects, to renovate some of utilities mentioned above.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you tell us that you were the commander of the mission and that your duty was to organise the work for your missions so they could perform their tasks, can you tell us, who participated -- or rather, whom did you hire and whom did you incorporate in the performance of your missions?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY MOROZ
utterances.text: So when our section got information that somewhere an object, either electricity line or water line is broken, our chief inspected -- section chief inspected that together with a specialist -- a civilian specialist and planned that mission. When we -- when the section got permission from both sides -- agreement from both warring sides - I mean, both civilians and military, local commanders - I went to the spot, having working teams sometimes from Muslim side, sometimes from Serbian side, depending where and what type of job should be done. And we always had an escort by UNPROFOR forces. Usually it was two, three APC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, I wonder whether this would be a suitable moment to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, I would just like to ask you, Mr. Moroz, whether you feel that using the English language causes you any problem or whether you have any difficulties in understanding or difficulties in expressing yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me not. Probably you do not understand me well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be to the parties, whether they would -- I take it that the interpreters are able to understand the witness -- the English of the witness to such an extent that they are able to translate into French and B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the English booth cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have to switch to the French booth first, whether the French interpreters have any problem in -- Yes. And then Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps on your channel the interpreters could confirm that they are able to translate properly, and perhaps you could then convey the message to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then with the -- if the transcribers have no problem. But from what I saw of the transcript, I don't see that there is a problem. Ms. Mahindaratne, you would have no problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think it's not necessary that the Russian interpreters will come back tomorrow. But I would like to know: Whenever we need them, how much time would it take to have them in court again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will this afternoon discuss the matter with the translation services and see whether presence or being on standby would be sufficient and whether it's possible to organise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, for the next witness, I expect that we would need Russian interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I expect so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since Mr. Kruk is speaking, I do not know what he will say, what he will prefer. But I think we should have interpreters here, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least that they should be available. We'll -- on the organisational level, we'll see this afternoon what has to be done or not. You've been only in court for a very short time, Mr. Moroz. You will understand that this was not your whole testimony, so we would like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom. And may I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony, although small, you've given until now and the testimony still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
